identification.name: Devī Kavacam (Durgā Kavacam / Caṇḍī Kavacam), opening verses
identification.source: Devī Kavacam, verses 1–2, recited as an aṅga (ancillary text) before the Durgā Saptaśatī (Devī Māhātmya)
identification.tradition: Śākta; recited in the Caṇḍī-pāṭha / Navarātri tradition
identification.notes: These are the opening question-and-answer verses of the widely recited Devī Kavacam. Some printed colophons attribute the kavaca to the Varāha Purāṇa. It is not part of the thirteen chapters of the Devī Māhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa) itself. Verse numbering varies slightly between editions.

meaning_summary: The sage Mārkaṇḍeya asks Brahmā, the Grandsire, to teach him the supreme secret in the world, which gives complete protection to human beings and has not been told to anyone. Brahmā replies that there is a most secret and holy teaching, beneficial to all beings: the kavaca (protective armour) of the Devī. He tells the great sage to listen to it.

story.speaker: Mārkaṇḍeya (question); Brahmā (answer)
story.listener: Brahmā (addressed as Pitāmaha); Mārkaṇḍeya (addressed as Vipra and Mahāmuni)
story.frame: A dialogue in which the sage Mārkaṇḍeya asks Brahmā for a secret means of protection, and Brahmā reveals the Devī's kavaca.
story.legend: In the text itself, Mārkaṇḍeya asks Brahmā to teach him the supreme secret in the world, one that gives every kind of protection to people and has never been told to anyone. Brahmā answers that the most secret teaching, which benefits all beings, is the holy kavaca of the Devī, and tells the great sage to hear it.

lines.english: That which is the supreme secret in the world,
which gives complete protection to human beings,
which has not been told to anyone —
tell that to me, O Grandsire (Brahmā).
There is, O Brahmin, a most secret teaching,
it is the holy kavaca (armour) of the Devī.
Listen to it, O great sage.

caution: This is only the opening frame (the question and Brahmā's reply), not the body of the kavaca. Many editions place a viniyoga before these verses, commonly naming Brahmā as ṛṣi, anuṣṭubh as metre and Cāmuṇḍā as deity. That viniyoga is not in the supplied text, so it has been left empty here; please check it against your edition. The source attribution in colophons varies, and some name the Varāha Purāṇa; teachers should check the edition they use. The initial 'ॐ' is a recitation convention, not part of the verse.
